CausalChain: Viral infection or stress -> Increased tRF production in host cells -> Packaging of specific tRFs into exosomes -> Exosomal release and uptake by neighboring immune cells -> tRF-mediated alteration of translation machinery (e.g., displacement of initiation factors/RBPs such as YBX1) -> Reduced translation of antiviral proteins -> Enhanced viral replication
Hypothesis: Exosome‐mediated delivery of stress-induced tRNA-derived fragments alters the translational machinery of recipient immune cells, reducing antiviral protein synthesis and thereby promoting viral replication.
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the multifaceted roles of tRNA‐derived fragments (tRFs) in regulating gene expression through interactions with mRNAs, ribosomes, and RNA‐binding proteins. Building on these insights, we propose a novel hypothesis that exosome‐mediated transfer of stress‐induced tRFs modulates the translational landscape of recipient immune cells, ultimately dampening innate antiviral responses and promoting viral replication. This paradigm suggests that under conditions of viral infection, cells produce specific tRFs that are packaged into exosomes and dispatched to neighboring immune cells. Within these target cells, the tRFs alter ribosome biogenesis and displace key initiation factors or RNA-binding proteins involved in antiviral cytokine translation, thereby creating a local environment that facilitates viral survival and spread. This hypothesis provides a framework for investigating how intercellular communication via tRF‐laden exosomes contributes to the complex interplay between viral infection, cellular stress responses, and host immunity.
